claims.text: Applying a thin Ni coating to tungsten particles before W–Cu composite fabrication will increase the composite's overall thermal conductivity relative to an uncoated control.
The Ni interlayer will reduce interfacial thermal resistance between tungsten and copper.
The Ni-coated composite will maintain mechanical durability or strength comparable to an otherwise similar uncoated W–Cu composite.
The Ni-coated composite will maintain irradiation resistance comparable to an otherwise similar uncoated W–Cu composite.
A Ni interlayer will produce more coherent and intimate contact at the W–Cu interface.
More coherent and intimate W–Cu interfacial contact will reduce phonon scattering at the interface.
More coherent and intimate W–Cu interfacial contact will reduce electron scattering at the interface.
The Ni interlayer will improve the wettability of tungsten by copper.
The Ni interlayer will improve bonding between tungsten and copper.
Lower W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance will facilitate heat transfer across the constituent phases.
A sufficiently thin Ni layer will not impair mechanical load transfer in the W–Cu composite.
A sufficiently thin Ni layer will not degrade under the stated irradiation conditions.
Sintering or hot pressing at 1000–1200 °C can ensure good bonding in the proposed Ni-coated W–Cu composite.
Formation of an extensive Ni-containing third phase could compromise the mechanical integrity of the composite.
The Ni layer could undergo a phase transformation under irradiation.
Extreme irradiation conditions or abnormal thermal cycles could destabilize the Ni layer.
Prior work on interfacial engineering in metal-matrix composites supports improved thermal transport through enhanced interface bonding.
